paras: The killing of Tom Jones at Louisville, Mississippi, was the fatal shooting of Tom Jones by F. L. Jones, a local photographer, in front of a Louisville store in early July 1882. Wire dispatches reported that a large crowd threatened to lynch the killer as he was taken to jail, and that a strong guard prevented it. He was convicted of murder at the next circuit court and sentenced to hang, then granted an appeal on the day set for his execution.

According to a letter from a Louisville doctor printed in the Kosciusko Messenger, the quarrel began over a young lady: Tom Jones said that F. L. Jones had made certain remarks about her, which F. L. Jones denied. The wire reports described the victim as 'a boy' and said the photographer had already killed four men.

When the two were brought face to face and Tom Jones held to his statement, F. L. Jones drew a pistol and fired in front of Dr. Woodward's store. The letter said he fired five times, twice into the chest as Tom stood and three more times after he fell, and that the victim lived about two hours. A man named John Blair struck F. L. Jones in the forehead with a brickbat, breaking the outer plate of his skull.

A special dispatch from Louisville said the killer was arrested soon afterward and 'with difficulty taken to jail, a large crowd following and threatening to lynch him.' A Jackson dispatch said that 'a strong guard prevented lynching'; the local letter mentioned only that Jones was under arrest.

The Winston County circuit court, which closed on July 14, convicted Jones of murder and sentenced him to be hanged on September 1. A Louisville dispatch of September 1 reported that he had been granted an appeal to the state Supreme Court that day. No report of the appeal's outcome appears in the coverage.

Mississippi papers carried the story first as a local item: The Comet of Jackson reprinted the Kosciusko Messenger's account on July 8, and the Brookhaven Ledger ran a longer version on July 13, neither mentioning a lynching threat. The national wire, dated July 10, presented the killing as a criminal curiosity under headlines such as 'A Photographer's Fifth Murder' and 'FOUR MURDERS', and called it a shooting 'in cold blood'.

A one-line version, saying he was 'only saved from lynching by a strong guard', ran in miscellaneous and crime columns of weeklies from Michigan to Dakota and Missouri through July 20. None of the reports gave the race of either man, and the Grenada Sentinel called them 'Mr. J. L. Jones' and 'Mr. Tom Jones'.

The local letter, printed in Jackson on July 8, placed the shooting on 'last Monday evening', while the July 10 wire dispatches said 'this morning' or 'yesterday'. Because the local account appeared before the wire and a July 15 court report put the killing 'two weeks since', the earlier date, probably July 3, is the better supported. Two Mississippi reports of the conviction gave the killer's initials as 'J. L.' rather than 'F. L.'

reader.title: Killing of Tom Jones at Louisville, Mississippi
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A homicide by one man in a personal quarrel, after which a crowd threatened to lynch the arrested killer (A4, A3); the papers state no race for either man, and nothing marks this as anti-Black violence (A1, A15).
A crowd threatened to lynch F. L. Jones after he killed Tom Jones, but a guard got him to jail (A4, A3); he was later tried, convicted and granted an appeal (A14, A16). No one was killed by a mob.

The local letter (A1, A7), the wire dispatches (A2, A3, A4) and the later court reports (A14, A15, A16) agree that F. L. Jones shot Tom Jones and was arrested; only the wire reports mention the lynching threat.

accounts.gist: Tom Jones said F. L. Jones had made remarks about a young lady; when they met face to face and Tom held to it, F. L. Jones drew a pistol and fired five times. Jones is under arrest; no lynching threat is mentioned.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: F. L. Jones 'became enraged' at a boy and shot him dead; he was taken to jail with difficulty as a crowd threatened to lynch him, and a strong guard prevented it.

accounts.label: Court report
accounts.gist: Jones was convicted of murder at the July term and sentenced to hang September 1, then granted an appeal.

framing.detail: National papers ran the dispatch under headlines counting his killings ('A Photographer's Fifth Murder', 'FOUR MURDERS') and called the shooting 'in cold blood'.
Mississippi papers printed a local letter about a quarrel over a young lady and later the conviction, without mentioning any lynching threat.

conflicts.note: The local letter appeared in The Comet on July 8, so the killing came before the July 10 dispatches; the July 15 court report's 'two weeks since' also points to early July. The local account is better evidence on the date.
Most reports, including the September report, give F. L.
